definition: Time-inhomogeneous hidden Bernoulli model (TI-HBM) is an alternative to hidden Markov model (HMM) for automatic speech recognition.
details: Contrary to HMM, the state transition process in TI-HBM is not a Markov-dependent process, rather it is a generalized Bernoulli (an independent) process. This difference leads to elimination of dynamic programming at state-level in TI-HBM decoding process. Thus, the computational complexity of TI-HBM for probability evaluation and state estimation is O ( N L ) {\displaystyle O(NL)} (instead of O ( N 2 L ) {\displaystyle O(N^{2}L)} in the HMM case, where N {\displaystyle N} and L {\displaystyle L} are number of states and observation sequence length respectively). The TI-HBM is able to model acoustic-unit duration (e.g. phone/word duration) by using a built-in parameter named survival probability. The TI-HBM is simpler and faster than HMM in a phoneme recognition task, but its performance is comparable to HMM. For details, see [1] or [2].

explainer.lead: TI-HBM is an alternative to the hidden Markov model for automatic speech recognition. It matters because it removes state-level dynamic programming, cutting decoding cost.

tiers.eli5: A normal speech model assumes each step depends on the one before, like a board game where your next move depends on where you just landed. This model instead treats each step as independent, which makes the maths much cheaper.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a cheaper decoding alternative to HMMs in speech recognition; a pitfall is that dropping Markov dependence changes the modelling assumptions, so gains come with a different probability structure.
tiers.paperLevel: In TI-HBM the state transition process is a generalised Bernoulli (independent) process rather than a Markov process, eliminating dynamic programming at state level and reducing probability evaluation and state estimation complexity to O(NL) instead of the HMM's O(N^2 L).

explainer.example: Because state transitions are independent, probability evaluation and state estimation scale as O(NL) rather than O(N^2 L), a direct saving as N and L grow.
